set1.q: Which set of findings defines MGUS (monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance)?
opts: An M-protein above 3 g/dL with 10-60% marrow plasma cells and no myeloma-defining events is smoldering myeloma. Tell: higher numbers without CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions) features mean smoldering.
Plasma cells 10% or more with bone lesions
Plasma cells of 10% or more plus a CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions) feature such as bone lesions defines multiple myeloma. Tell: an end-organ feature means myeloma.
A lymphocyte count below 5,000 with no nodes, organomegaly or cytopenias is monoclonal B lymphocytosis. Tell: that is a lymphocyte clone, not a plasma cell clone.
M-protein under 3 g/dL, plasma cells under 10%

Correct. MGUS (monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance) is by definition asymptomatic: M-protein below 3 g/dL, clonal bone marrow plasma cells below 10% and no myeloma-defining characteristics. It progresses to myeloma at about 1% per year.

set1.q: What causes the hypercalcemia of multiple myeloma?
opts: Tumor lysis releases potassium, phosphorus and uric acid, not calcium from bone. Tell: myeloma calcium comes from bone resorption.
Renal dysfunction in myeloma comes from light chain and calcium phosphate deposition; the calcium itself comes from bone. Tell: osteoclasts are the source.

Correct. Myeloma activates osteoclasts, resulting in calcium release into the bloodstream. Hypercalcemia causes constipation, increased thirst, urinary frequency and nausea, and the same bone resorption makes punched-out lesions.
Light chain and calcium phosphate deposition cause the renal dysfunction of myeloma, not the hypercalcemia. Tell: light chains hit the kidney; osteoclasts release the calcium.

opts: Epstein-Barr virus is strongly tied to endemic Burkitt lymphoma and suspected in Hodgkin lymphoma. Tell: a gastric marginal zone lymphoma points to H. pylori.
Human T-lymphotropic virus 1 is associated with adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma. Tell: a T-cell virus goes with a T-cell lymphoma, not a gastric B-cell one.

Correct. Gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma, the extranodal marginal zone subtype, is associated with Helicobacter pylori in two thirds of cases. Extranodal disease is the most common marginal zone subtype.

opts: Helicobacter pylori gastritis is tied to gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma in two thirds of cases, not to a reactive lymphocytosis. Tell: H. pylori means gastric lymphoma.
Hepatitis C is associated with splenic marginal zone lymphoma and is a non-Hodgkin lymphoma risk factor, not the named cause of atypical lymphocytosis. Tell: the mimic named is pertussis.
Lyme disease is listed among the chronic infections that raise non-Hodgkin lymphoma risk. Tell: a reactive lymphocytosis mimic here is pertussis.

set1.q: Burkitt lymphoma is associated with upregulation of which gene?
opts: Correct. Burkitt lymphoma is associated with MYC (myelocytomatosis oncogene) upregulation, which stimulates cell growth and division. That explains a swelling that can visibly enlarge over one day.
BCL-2 (B-cell lymphoma 2) is moved to chromosome 14 by t(14;18) in follicular lymphoma, preventing cell death. Tell: the cell-death gene is follicular; Burkitt is the growth gene.
Cyclin D1 translocation t(11;14) identifies mantle cell lymphoma. Tell: cyclin D1 is mantle cell.
MYD88 (myeloid differentiation primary response 88) mutation is found in about 90% of lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. Tell: that marks Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, not Burkitt.

set1.q: Hodgkin lymphoma has a bimodal incidence. Which two age groups are affected?
opts: Correct. Hodgkin lymphoma has a bimodal incidence, peaking in adults in their 20s and in adults over 60 years old. Older patients also have inferior results with treatment.
Early childhood is not one of the peaks; the younger peak is adults in their 20s. Tell: young adults, not toddlers.
The peaks are earlier: adults in their 20s and adults over 60. Tell: one peak in young adulthood, one past 60.
The younger peak in the 20s is right, but the second is in adults over 60, not the 40s. Tell: the older peak is past 60.

set1.q: What are Reed-Sternberg cells?
opts: Correct. Hodgkin lymphoma is a type of B-cell lymphoma characterized by few malignant cells, the Reed-Sternberg cells, which are binucleated, neoplastic B cells, set among numerous immune effector cells.
Benign macrophages clearing dying lymphoma cells give the starry sky appearance of Burkitt lymphoma. Tell: macrophages are the Burkitt stars; Reed-Sternberg cells are the malignant cells of Hodgkin.
Clonal plasma cells, terminally differentiated B cells, define the plasma cell disorders such as multiple myeloma. Tell: Reed-Sternberg cells are binucleated B cells, not plasma cells.
Neoplastic T cells make up the T-cell lymphomas. Hodgkin lymphoma is a type of B-cell lymphoma. Tell: the Reed-Sternberg cell is a binucleated B cell.

set1.q: How is chronic lymphocytic leukemia most often first discovered?
opts: A mass that grows visibly over one day describes Burkitt lymphoma, a very aggressive lymphoma. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia nodes are painless, firm and mobile, and the disease is often silent. Tell: rapid growth means Burkitt.

Correct. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is frequently diagnosed while the patient is asymptomatic, on routine blood work that shows a lymphocytosis. Symptoms, when present, come from nodes, cytopenias or B symptoms.
Only 5-10% of patients develop B symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, fevers), so they are not the usual route to diagnosis. Tell: most patients have no symptoms at all when the count is found.
Thrombocytopenia can cause easy bruising and bleeding, but most patients are asymptomatic when diagnosed. Tell: bleeding is a cytopenia symptom, not the common first clue.

set1.q: What is the main focus of treatment in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma?
opts: Correct. Treatments for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides) focus on the cutaneous manifestations, because there is often no visceral involvement. The aggressive Sezary form brings severe itching that lowers quality of life.
Visceral involvement is often absent in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, so it is not the main target. Tell: the skin is the disease.
The lesions resemble fungal infections but are lymphoma, so antifungals do not treat them. Tell: fungal-looking skin lesions here are T-cell lymphoma.
Rituximab targets cluster of differentiation 20 on B cells; T cells do not express it, so T-cell lymphoma regimens omit it. Tell: no rituximab for T-cell disease.

set1.q: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma cells express which pair of cluster of differentiation markers?
opts: Cluster of differentiation 19 belongs to the chronic lymphocytic leukemia pair (with 5). Tell: Hodgkin pairs 30 with 15.

Correct. Classical Hodgkin lymphoma expresses cluster of differentiation 15 and cluster of differentiation 30. The diagnosis itself is made by excisional lymph node biopsy, avoiding fine needle aspiration.
Coexpression of cluster of differentiation 19 and 5 identifies chronic lymphocytic leukemia on flow cytometry. Tell: 19 and 5 are the leukemia; 15 and 30 are Hodgkin.
Cluster of differentiation 20 is the rituximab target on B cells and 5 is part of the chronic lymphocytic leukemia pair. Tell: classical Hodgkin is 15 and 30.

set1.q: How is a single-node, non-aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma treated?
opts: Multi-drug chemotherapy is the approach to aggressive B-cell lymphomas. Tell: one node and non-aggressive means radiation.
Autologous transplant improves survival in transplant-eligible multiple myeloma. Tell: transplant belongs to myeloma; a single indolent node gets radiation.
Allopurinol and fluids prevent tumor lysis syndrome before aggressive lymphoma treatment; they do not treat the lymphoma. Tell: prevention, not therapy.

Correct. Management depends heavily on subtype and presentation; a single-node, non-aggressive lymphoma is treated with radiation. Aggressive B-cell lymphomas instead get multi-drug chemotherapy with rituximab.

set1.q: What proportion of Hodgkin lymphoma patients are alive at 5 years?
opts: About 50% is the cure rate of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Tell: Hodgkin is generally curable, over 90% at 5 years.
About 60% is the 5-year relative survival of multiple myeloma. Tell: Hodgkin lymphoma does better, over 90%.
About 78% is the relative 5-year survival of lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. Tell: Hodgkin lymphoma survival exceeds 90%.
Correct. Hodgkin lymphoma is generally curable, with more than 90% of patients alive at 5 years. Relapse after first-line treatment may require allogeneic stem cell transplant.

set1.q: Which T-cell lymphoma is associated with human T-lymphotropic virus 1?
opts: Mycosis fungoides is cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, skin lesions that resemble fungal infection. Tell: skin lesions mean mycosis fungoides; the viral link belongs to adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma.
Correct. Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma is very aggressive, associated with human T-lymphotropic virus 1, and more common in the Caribbean, Central America and South America.
Anaplastic large cell lymphoma is an aggressive T-cell lymphoma but carries no viral link on the list. Tell: the virus-linked type is adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma.
Hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma is another listed subtype without the viral association. Tell: the Caribbean, virus-linked type is adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma.

set1.q: How much is Hodgkin lymphoma risk raised in a same-sex sibling of a patient?
opts: Twice is the male excess in chronic lymphocytic leukemia, not the Hodgkin sibling risk. Tell: Hodgkin sibling risk is tenfold.
Four times understates the sibling risk, which is 10 times. Tell: the same-sex sibling figure is ten.
Correct. Same-sex siblings of a patient have a 10 times increased risk of also developing Hodgkin lymphoma. Epstein-Barr virus is a suspected risk factor, found in 40-50% of cases.
Fifty times overstates it; the increase for a same-sex sibling is 10 times. Tell: a tenfold rise.

set1.q: Which regimen is an example of multi-drug therapy for aggressive B-cell lymphoma?
opts: Venetoclax plus obinutuzumab for a fixed duration

A B-cell lymphoma 2 inhibitor such as venetoclax combined with a monoclonal antibody for a fixed duration is a chronic lymphocytic leukemia approach. Tell: that is a leukemia combination; aggressive lymphoma gets rituximab with CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone).
Rituximab plus CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone)

Correct. Aggressive B-cell lymphomas are often treated with multi-drug chemotherapy such as R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, prednisone). Rituximab is the anti-cluster of differentiation 20 monoclonal antibody.
ABVD (doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine) without rituximab

ABVD (doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine) is the historical short-course chemotherapy for early Hodgkin lymphoma. Tell: that regimen is Hodgkin; rituximab with CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) is aggressive B-cell.
CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) without rituximab

CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) without rituximab is for T-cell lymphomas, which do not express cluster of differentiation 20. Tell: a B-cell lymphoma keeps the rituximab.

set1.q: About 80% of chronic lymphocytic leukemia cases arise from one of four chromosomal changes. Which is one of them?
opts: The t(4;14) translocation is a high-risk chromosomal abnormality in the myeloma staging table, not one of the four chronic lymphocytic leukemia changes. Tell: myeloma high-risk changes are translocations plus deletion 17p.

Correct. About 80% of cases result from loss or addition of chromosomal material in one of four abnormalities: deletion 13q, deletion 11q, trisomy 12 and deletion 17p. These are why cytogenetics matters for prognosis.

The t(14;18) translocation places the B-cell lymphoma 2 gene on chromosome 14 and prevents cell death in follicular lymphoma. Tell: chronic lymphocytic leukemia changes are deletions or a trisomy, not this translocation.
The t(11;14) translocation of the cyclin D1 gene identifies mantle cell lymphoma. Tell: the four chronic lymphocytic leukemia changes are deletion 13q, deletion 11q, trisomy 12 and deletion 17p.

opts: Cluster of differentiation 15 belongs to classical Hodgkin lymphoma, paired there with 30. Tell: the chronic lymphocytic leukemia pair is 19 and 5.

Correct. Flow cytometry shows coexpression of cluster of differentiation 19 and cluster of differentiation 5 on the lymphocytes, which identifies the clonal B-cell population that confirms chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
Cluster of differentiation 15 and 30 are expressed by classical Hodgkin lymphoma. Tell: 15 and 30 mean Hodgkin; 19 and 5 mean chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
Cluster of differentiation 20 is the target of rituximab on B cells, and 30 is a Hodgkin lymphoma marker; this pair is not the leukemia signature. Tell: the coexpressed pair here is 19 with 5.

set1.q: Which non-Hodgkin lymphoma patients may need hospitalization for treatment?
opts: Low-grade B-cell lymphoma treated with rituximab is managed as an outpatient. Tell: hospital care is for aggressive disease with deranged electrolytes.
Correct. Aggressive lymphomas with electrolyte abnormalities may require hospitalization; otherwise treatment is often outpatient. Burkitt lymphoma requires rapid transfer of care.
Indolent disease such as follicular lymphoma is often watched or treated intermittently as an outpatient. Tell: admission is for aggressive disease with electrolyte problems.

set1.q: Why is fine needle aspiration avoided when lymphoma is suspected?
opts: Seeding is not the reason given; aspiration is avoided because it cannot show the node's architecture and may miss the diagnosis. Tell: the problem is too little tissue.
Tumor lysis syndrome comes from rapid tumor breakdown, spontaneously in aggressive lymphoma or with treatment, not from a needle. Tell: the concern is a missed diagnosis.
The reason given is diagnostic, not procedural: the needle sample loses the node architecture. Tell: architecture decides the method.

Correct. Fine needle aspiration is avoided because an excisional biopsy is required to observe the lymph node architecture, and aspiration may miss the diagnosis. Biopsy is reserved for significant (2 cm), persistent and progressively enlarging nodes.

set1.q: At what rate does monoclonal B lymphocytosis progress to chronic lymphocytic leukemia?
opts: Correct. Monoclonal B lymphocytosis, a count below 5,000 with no nodes, organomegaly, cytopenias or symptoms, progresses to chronic lymphocytic leukemia at a rate of 1-2% per year.
About 10% per year is the progression rate of smoldering myeloma to multiple myeloma. Tell: 10% belongs to smoldering myeloma; 1-2% to monoclonal B lymphocytosis.
A quarter per year overstates the risk; monoclonal B lymphocytosis progresses at only 1-2% per year. Tell: it is a low-risk precursor.
Above 50% within 2 years is the risk in some high-risk smoldering myeloma groups, not the yearly rate for monoclonal B lymphocytosis. Tell: 1-2% per year here.

opts: Thirty-five is the age below which sporadic Burkitt lymphoma almost always occurs. Tell: myeloma is a disease of older adults, mostly over 65.
Forty-five is too young; most myeloma diagnoses are over 65. Tell: think of an older adult.

Correct. Myeloma risk increases with age, and most diagnoses are made over age 65. It is a disease of older adults, also more common in African Americans and in those with prior monoclonal gammopathy or smoldering myeloma.
Eighty-five overshoots; most diagnoses come after 65. Tell: the threshold is 65.

opts: Venetoclax is the B-cell lymphoma 2 inhibitor, combined with monoclonal antibodies for a fixed duration. Tell: the kinase inhibitors end in -brutinib.
Obinutuzumab is a monoclonal antibody, listed with rituximab and ofatumumab. Tell: monoclonal antibodies end in -mab; the kinase inhibitors end in -brutinib.
Allopurinol is a hypouricemic agent given with fluids before aggressive lymphoma treatment to prevent tumor lysis syndrome. Tell: it prevents a complication; it is not a targeted leukemia therapy.

Correct. The Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors are ibrutinib, acalabrutinib and zanubrutinib, usually given continuously when used as monotherapy. They are one of the targeted therapies for chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

set1.q: What is needed to assign a Rai stage in chronic lymphocytic leukemia?
opts: A marrow biopsy is not needed for Rai staging and is usually not needed for diagnosis either. Tell: the stage comes from the exam and the blood counts.
Cytogenetics inform prognosis and some treatment choices but are not part of the Rai stage. Tell: Rai uses nodes, organs, hemoglobin and platelets, not chromosomes.

Correct. Rai staging does not require advanced imaging; it can be performed with the physical exam and labs, by checking for lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, anemia and thrombocytopenia alongside the lymphocytosis.

Marginal zone lymphomas make up 5-17% of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Tell: a minority subtype; the adult leader is diffuse large B-cell.
Correct. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma in adults. It is aggressive, presenting as a fast-growing mass and/or B symptoms, and about 50% are cured.

Follicular lymphoma is the most common indolent histology, not the most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma overall in adults. Tell: indolent leader is follicular; overall adult leader is diffuse large B-cell.

M-protein over 3 g/dL, plasma cells 10-60%, no CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions)

Nodes that grow within a day
Visible growth over one day is Burkitt lymphoma. Tell: same-day growth means Burkitt; alcohol-related pain means Hodgkin.

Helicobacter pylori is linked to gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma, the extranodal subtype. Tell: H. pylori is the stomach; hepatitis C is the spleen.
Human immunodeficiency virus is tied to immunodeficiency-associated Burkitt lymphoma and is a general lymphoma risk. Tell: the splenic marginal zone association is hepatitis C.

Stage 2 is two or more node regions on the same side of the diaphragm. Tell: crossing the diaphragm moves it to stage 3.

opts: Correct. The diagnosis is confirmed by flow cytometry, which identifies the clonal B-cell population, coexpressing the cluster of differentiation markers 19 and 5. A bone marrow biopsy is usually not required.
A bone marrow biopsy is usually not required to diagnose chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: the blood itself is examined by flow cytometry to show the clone.

Excisional lymph node biopsy is how a lymphoma is diagnosed, because the node architecture must be seen. This leukemia is confirmed from the blood. Tell: node biopsy is for lymphoma; flow cytometry is for this leukemia.

Serum protein electrophoresis shows the monoclonal protein of multiple myeloma and the other plasma cell disorders. Tell: a monoclonal protein means a plasma cell disorder; a clonal B-cell population on flow means chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

Correct. Monoclonal B lymphocytosis is an elevated absolute lymphocyte count but below 5,000, with no lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, cytopenias or other symptoms. It progresses to chronic lymphocytic leukemia at 1-2% per year.

Hairy cell leukemia is another lymphoproliferative disorder in the differential, distinguished by morphology and immunophenotype. Tell: a small clone below 5,000 with no findings is the precursor state, monoclonal B lymphocytosis.

set2.q: How is tumor lysis syndrome prevented before treating an aggressive lymphoma?

Tumor lysis syndrome requires aggressive intravenous fluid hydration; restricting fluids would worsen crystal precipitation. Tell: give fluids, never restrict them.

Correct. Tumor lysis syndrome should be anticipated in aggressive lymphoma, and patients are given allopurinol (a hypouricemic agent) and fluids in advance. Patients are told to drink plenty of fluids and take allopurinol on starting treatment.

T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia is the name for rare mature T-cell leukemias, not a transformation of the B-cell disease. Tell: Richter transformation produces an aggressive B-cell lymphoma.

set2.q: About what share of non-Hodgkin lymphomas are B-cell lymphomas?
opts: Four percent is the share of all new cancer diagnoses in the United States that are non-Hodgkin lymphoma, not the B-cell fraction. Tell: 4% is of all cancers; 85% is the B-cell share of these lymphomas.
Fifteen percent is the T-cell or natural killer-cell share, not the B-cell share. Tell: B-cell lymphomas are the large majority.
The split is not even; B-cell types make up about 85%. Tell: the T-cell and natural killer-cell types are the minority at 15%.

Correct. About 85% of non-Hodgkin lymphomas are B-cell and 15% are T-cell or natural killer-cell. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is a diverse group of lymphoid malignancies that present frequently with lymphadenopathy.

set2.q: In the Rai classification, lymphocytosis with lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly, with normal hemoglobin and platelets, is which stage?
opts: Stage I is lymphocytosis with lymphadenopathy only. Tell: an enlarged spleen counts as organomegaly and moves the stage to II.
Correct. Rai stage II is lymphocytosis, lymphadenopathy and organomegaly, defined as hepatomegaly and/or splenomegaly. With no anemia and no thrombocytopenia, the stage does not rise to III or IV.
Stage III requires anemia. Tell: the hemoglobin is normal, so organomegaly alone stops at stage II.
Stage IV requires thrombocytopenia. Tell: the platelets are normal, so the stage cannot reach IV.

set2.q: Which caution applies when starting therapy for Burkitt lymphoma?
opts: Bleomycin pulmonary toxicity is a concern in Hodgkin lymphoma regimens. Tell: the Burkitt caution is rapid tumor breakdown.
Hyperviscosity is a complication of immunoglobulin M in lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. Tell: Burkitt's danger at the start of therapy is tumor lysis.
Richter transformation is chronic lymphocytic leukemia turning into an aggressive B-cell lymphoma, not a treatment caution for Burkitt. Tell: think tumor lysis.

Correct. Caution is needed when initiating therapy because of tumor lysis syndrome; it can even occur spontaneously in highly aggressive lymphomas such as Burkitt. Fluids and allopurinol are given in advance.

set2.q: An M-protein of 1.5 g/dL, clonal marrow plasma cells of 4% and no anemia, bone lesions or renal failure fit which disorder?
opts: Smoldering myeloma needs an M-protein above 3 g/dL and 10-60% marrow plasma cells. Tell: 1.5 g/dL and 4% are both below those lines.
Active multiple myeloma with end-organ damage
Myeloma needs 10% or more marrow plasma cells or a plasmacytoma plus a CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions) feature. Tell: 4% and no end-organ damage rule it out.
ruled out by a stated finding
Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia is a lymphoma producing immunoglobulin M with hyperviscosity. Tell: no immunoglobulin M or hyperviscosity is given; the numbers fit the low-level plasma cell disorder.

Correct. An M-protein below 3 g/dL (1.5 g/dL), clonal marrow plasma cells below 10% (4%) and no myeloma-defining characteristics meet every part of MGUS (monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance), which progresses at about 1% per year.

set2.q: Which criterion diagnoses multiple myeloma?
opts: Marrow plasma cells of 10% or more with a CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions) feature

Correct. Multiple myeloma is diagnosed by bone marrow plasma cells of 10% or more, or a biopsy-proven plasmacytoma, plus one or more CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions) features. A monoclonal protein is characteristic.
Marrow plasma cells under 10% with no CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions) feature

Plasma cells under 10% with no myeloma-defining feature and a small monoclonal protein describe monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance. Tell: low cells and no CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions) means the premalignant state.
Marrow plasma cells of 10% or more and a high monoclonal protein alone

Plasma cells of 10-60% with a monoclonal protein above 3 g/dL and no myeloma-defining event is smoldering myeloma. Tell: without a CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions) feature it is smoldering, not myeloma.
An absolute lymphocyte count above 5,000 for 3 months

A lymphocyte count above 5,000 for 3 months is the blood criterion for chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: lymphocytes are the leukemia; marrow plasma cells plus CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions) are myeloma.

set2.q: What produces the starry sky appearance of Burkitt lymphoma?
opts: Clonal plasma cells in the marrow define the plasma cell disorders such as multiple myeloma. Tell: plasma cells mean myeloma.

Correct. The starry sky appearance is sheets of lymphoma cells with benign macrophages that are clearing out the dying lymphoma cells. The pale macrophages are the stars against the dark sheet of tumor.
Binucleated neoplastic B cells (Reed-Sternberg cells) among many immune cells define Hodgkin lymphoma. Tell: few large binucleated cells mean Hodgkin; macrophages in sheets mean Burkitt.
Clusters of packed follicles are the microscopy of follicular lymphoma. Tell: follicles mean follicular; starry sky means Burkitt.

set2.topic: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia: who and why
set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hematological malignancies: 1. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia 2. Chronic myelogenous leukemia 3. Polycythemia vera a. primary b. secondary 4. Multiple myeloma 5. Myelodysplasia (myelodysplastic syndromes)
set2.q: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a proliferation of which cell type?
opts: Correct. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a proliferative leukemia of mature B-cell lymphocytes found in the blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes and spleen. Mutagenesis occurs in mature B cells, which is why the disease presents as a clonal population.
Immature blasts describe an acute leukemia, not this chronic disease, whose cells are mature B lymphocytes. Tell: chronic means mature cells accumulating; acute means blasts.

Mature T-cell leukemias exist but are rare and carry another name, T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia itself is a B-cell disease. Tell: the common chronic lymphocytic leukemia is B-cell; the T-cell form is rare and named separately.

Clonal plasma cells, terminally differentiated B cells, define the plasma cell disorders such as multiple myeloma, not chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Tell: plasma cells make a monoclonal protein; this leukemia is a lymphocytosis of mature B cells.

set2.q: When used as monotherapy, how long is a Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor usually given?
opts: A fixed duration describes venetoclax combined with monoclonal antibodies. Tell: kinase inhibitor monotherapy keeps going.
No count-based stopping point is given; the drug is usually continuous as monotherapy. Tell: monotherapy is open-ended.
Kinase inhibitor monotherapy is not stopped when symptoms improve; it is usually continuous and the pill may be indefinite. Tell: continuous, not symptom-guided.

Correct. Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors (ibrutinib, acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib) are usually continuous when used as monotherapy; pill therapy may be indefinite. Time-limited courses belong to the combination regimens.

set2.q: In the Hodgkin lymphoma work-up, what is the chest X-ray used for?
opts: Tumor lysis syndrome is ruled out with chemistries, particularly electrolytes. Tell: blood tests for tumor lysis; chest X-ray for the mediastinum.

Correct. A chest X-ray rules out a mediastinal mass or adenopathy. The rest of the work-up is excisional biopsy, a complete blood count, chemistries for tumor lysis, lactate dehydrogenase and a bone marrow biopsy.
The diagnosis is made by excisional lymph node biopsy. Tell: imaging looks for the mass; the excised node gives the diagnosis.
Punched-out osteolytic lesions are a multiple myeloma finding, classically imaged with whole-body computed tomography. Tell: lytic bone lesions mean myeloma.

set2.q: How does the R-ISS (Revised International Staging System) stage affect myeloma treatment decisions?
opts: It decides when to start treatment
Starting treatment by stage describes how the Rai stage may guide chronic lymphocytic leukemia therapy. Tell: myeloma staging is prognostic only.
It sets the number of drugs given
Newly diagnosed patients get a 3- or 4-drug regimen; the stage does not broadly change that. Tell: R-ISS (Revised International Staging System) is about prognosis.

Correct. The R-ISS (Revised International Staging System) describes prognostic groups from chromosomal abnormalities, proliferative status and the impact on normal protein production. While prognostic, it does not impact treatment decisions broadly.
Transplant candidacy is a separate decision; the staging system does not broadly drive treatment. Tell: R-ISS (Revised International Staging System) predicts, it does not prescribe.

set2.q: Which symptoms reflect the hypercalcemia of multiple myeloma?
opts: Pain in the back, chest or pelvis reflects bone lesions, the B of CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions). Tell: bone pain is the B; constipation and thirst are the C.

Correct. In the CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions) features, hypercalcemia causes constipation, increased thirst, urinary frequency and nausea. Renal insufficiency causes swelling and anemia causes fatigue and shortness of breath.
Swelling is the symptom linked to renal insufficiency, the R of CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions). Tell: swelling is renal; constipation and thirst are calcium.
Fatigue and shortness of breath reflect anemia, the A of CRAB (calcium, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lesions). Tell: those are anemia symptoms, not calcium symptoms.
